description: We are a multidisciplinary team and NASA Space Apps Global Nominees from last year, with experience across multiple projects and individual hackathon wins. Our interests span AI/ML, software engineering, cloud, DevOps, data science and space technology. We combine technical execution, creative thinking and research-driven problem-solving to build practical, innovative solutions. This year, we aim to push boundaries, explore NASA's open data and tackle real-world challenges.
summary:
LUMEN is a free planner that runs in your browser and answers a simple question about the Moon's south pole: when will a lander have sunlight, when can it see Earth, and how confident can you be in those answers?

The pole is tricky because the Sun barely climbs above the horizon. A ridge only a fraction of a degree too tall can block it for days, and the usual smooth-sphere calculators miss that completely. So we took NASA's SPICE ephemeris data and combined it with horizon profiles built from LRO laser-altimeter terrain maps. You see a real skyline of the site with the Sun and Earth tracks drawn across it.

Planners can export a table of every sunlit, Earth-visible and communication window as CSV or JSON, and check Deep Space Network coverage. They can ask "what if we launch nine days late?" and compare several sites side by side. Event times come with uncertainty ranges from a Monte-Carlo analysis of the terrain data, so you can see how firm each number is.

Everything works offline after the first load, and a built-in helper, Ask LUMEN, explains any figure on screen in plain language.

Our goal is to help teams weigh sites and launch dates on real terrain before they commit a lander.
details:
What it does and how it works

LUMEN tells you when the Sun is up and when Earth is in view at a lunar landing site, and it does it fast enough to explore. The heavy lifting happens once, ahead of time. Then everything runs live in your browser.

In the build step, a Python pipeline turns NASA SPICE data into Sun and Earth positions in a Moon-fixed frame. It reads LRO LOLA terrain maps and traces the horizon at each site in 0.1° steps, out to 250 km, for four different solar-array heights. A Monte-Carlo run over 30 terrain variations gives each horizon an uncertainty. DSN station kernels give us the Moon elevation at Goldstone, Canberra and Madrid. All of it is saved as static files.

In the browser, a TypeScript engine in a Web Worker takes it from there. It interpolates the ephemeris, rotates it into the site's frame, checks the Sun's disk against the horizon, and finds sunrises, sunsets and Earth passes to within about 10 seconds. From those it builds windows, percentages, uncertainty bounds and a verdict. Every calculation also has a Python twin, and we compare the two on shared test cases to keep them in agreement. A service worker caches the app and its data, so after the first visit it works without a connection.

What you can do with it

- Orbit: a globe driven by the real ephemeris. Pick one of 13 sites or drop a pin anywhere.

- Stand here: a 360° skyline of the real terrain with the Sun and Earth paths across it, plus sunset and Earthset countdowns. A Windows Table lists every window with start, end, duration and peak elevation, and exports as CSV or JSON. You also get Earth pointing, range and light time, DSN station lanes, and a power and survival barcode.

- Slip explorer: slide the launch date and watch sunlight and DSN contact change.

- Compare: line up to four sites over the same 14 days.

- Ask LUMEN: press / and ask why a number is what it is. The answer is built from the live result, with no language model involved.

Why it matters

Planners and educators can weigh sites and launch dates on real terrain before anyone commits a lander. The numbers are exportable, the uncertainty is visible, and there is nothing to install. It is free and works anywhere, even offline.

What we built it with

- Frontend: React, Vite, TypeScript, Web Workers, Workbox for offline use, Vitest and Playwright.

- Pipeline: Python with NumPy, SciPy, Numba, rasterio, pyproj, SpiceyPy and Skyfield.

- Data: NASA NAIF SPICE, JPL Horizons for cross-checks, LRO LOLA terrain from the PGDA, Mazarico et al. (2011) illumination maps, and imagery from NASA SDO, EPIC/DSCOVR and LROC.

- Hardware: just a laptop. It deploys as a static site.

What makes it different

Most tools treat the Moon as a smooth ball. We draw the Sun and Earth against the site's actual horizon, which is what decides things near the pole. We also built the slip question into the app as its own view, because "we're late, what still works?" is what planners really ask. And Ask LUMEN explains each number from the live result, so the answers always match what's on screen.

What we kept in mind

We worked from correctness first: the browser engine and the Python pipeline are checked against each other, and the geometry is cross-checked against JPL Horizons. We designed for offline use from the start, with no live API on the demo path. We also cared about showing where each number comes from, so every figure has a "Why?" next to it and every image is credited.
